nodes.author: aakashgupta
nodes.text:
Wispr raised $81M at a $700M valuation in November. They hit $10M in revenue by October 2025 with a team under 50 people growing 40% month over month.

The "3x more accurate" claim needs unpacking. One independent benchmark put Wispr at 97.2% transcription accuracy versus 85-90% for Apple Dictation and 89-92% for Google Voice Typing. But Wispr's CEO measures a different metric entirely: the percentage of messages users send without making any edits. That accounts for tone, formatting, and context, like spelling "Bryan" correctly based on your contacts or adjusting formality between Slack and email. Edit-free output rate is a harder bar than word error rate, and it's the one that determines whether someone keeps using the product or goes back to typing.

This tells you everything about why Apple, Microsoft, and Google have failed here. They've bundled voice dictation free into every OS for over a decade. Nobody uses it, because 90% accuracy means a mistake in nearly every sentence. Users learn to associate voice input with frustration, and that association is almost impossible to reverse through incremental improvement. Wispr charges $12/month and 270 Fortune 500 companies are paying, which means the habit-formation threshold sits somewhere between 90% and 97%. Below that line, free isn't cheap enough. Above it, people will pay.

The average B2B SaaS company spends $702 to acquire a customer. At $12/month, that's a 4.8 year payback before churn. Paid acquisition breaks at a $144/year price point, which is why most PLG companies at this tier (Notion, Figma early days, Superhuman) lean on organic loops.

Wispr's is extreme even by those standards. 90% of growth is word of mouth. Kothari personally onboarded the first 500 users over Google Meet, watching facial expressions and mouse movements to find exact moments of delight, then engineered those moments into the product. He killed SEO entirely because "no one is searching for voice dictation." You can't run demand capture on a category most people assume is still broken. The Porsche challenge is the same logic at scale: a $250K product demo that shifts perception of a category written off for a decade.

Wispr was also the 8th product the team built internally. The first 7 were computer action tools similar to what OpenAI later shipped as Operator. People used them once a day if they remembered. Voice dictation stuck because people spend 90% of computer time consuming content or communicating. Massive surface area for a habit-forming input tool at $12/month.

The $700M valuation prices in a question. The organic loop works because the product is visible: someone dictating in a meeting generates curiosity. But that loop was built inside Silicon Valley, where every VC was already a daily user before the Series A. Kothari has said 95% of the population is the real market. The Android launch today and the enterprise push (125 new companies per week as of November) are both attempts to answer whether word-of-mouth scales when the early network stops being San Francisco tech workers.

nodes.author: aakashgupta
nodes.text:
Speaking is faster than typing. That’s why using speech AI is a hack.

From my debate days, I could speak at 281 WPM with 100% accuracy. But I’m so used to autocorrect that my typing was not only slow, it was inaccurate. 281 WPM dictation. 28 WPM typing. A 10x difference on the same person, producing the same output.

The average knowledge worker types at 40 WPM. Speaking speed averages 150 WPM. That’s a 3.75x gap between how fast you think and how fast you can get thoughts into a machine.

The keyboard has been the bottleneck for every knowledge worker for 50 years. We accepted it because built-in dictation was so bad it created more work than it saved. You’d spend 30 seconds dictating and 2 minutes fixing transcription errors.

What changed is the AI layer between your voice and the text field. Tools like Wispr Flow don’t just transcribe. They understand intent, strip filler words, and format contextually. The error correction problem that killed voice input for decades just disappeared.

Thanks to Wispr Flow for partnering on this post. I genuinely use it every day for drafting PRDs, writing newsletter content, and responding to Slack. It’s become invisible infrastructure in my workflow.

Think about what this means for daily output. A PM writing a PRD at 40 WPM spends 60-90 minutes typing a 3,000-word doc. At 4x speed with voice, that’s 15-22 minutes for the same output. A founder answering 50 emails a day reclaims an hour. A content creator producing 5,000 words of newsletter copy cuts a full morning down to 45 minutes.

The people who figure out the input layer first will simply produce more. More docs, more content, more decisions communicated clearly. Speed of output is a compounding advantage in knowledge work, and we’ve been leaving a 4-10x multiplier on the table because the keyboard felt “good enough.”

Try the challenge. You’ll see the gap instantly.

My lawyer friend just saw half her team get laid off.

These are top lawyers btw. Those that graduated from top law schools in the country, worked with the biggest names in the industry globally.

She pinged me asking how she could level up. The panic in her voice was real.

I’ve been hearing a lot on how AI won’t take jobs but create a ton of them.

I’m not seeing the tons getting created just as yet. I am, however, seeing a bunch of them across industries get canned.

So I wrote her a small note on how she can level up and get plugged in-

1. Help your current company make money- whatever your company does, optimize workflows, reduce costs, generate new leads- wherever you fit in, help the company get sharper 

2. Set out a dedicated budget to level up in every way- courses on AI won’t cut it- every day the space changes for the better - be on X/Reddit/ Hackernews/YT- become a consumption machine and apply your learnings 

3. Use AI for almost everything you do - you’ll fail at most things first, but it gets better. Get the Claude code max plan. 

4. Set automation workflows for yourself - use @interaction to remind you pay bills, order groceries, create content for you, journal daily 

5. Document everything- using @WisprFlow is a superpower. Any idea I have is a PRD in less than a minute with it, and an openclaw agent has a landing page, an app, and a sales funnel going at it

6. Surround yourself with crazy people who have their own agents running - You need a support group, one that’s just trying new things and sharing them openly. 
I’ve a group with @innercircle_so founding members where their agents are doing things all the time.

Do this for 30 days and the compounding effects will be visible. 

You might still lose the job you have.
But you will be able to create and capture value in the new agentic economy.

> Wispr Flow captures it all in real time, cleans out the filler words, formats it into actual paragraphs
> 15 minutes later i have a draft on my phone that reads like something i'd publish, not a messy transcript i need to spend an hour cleaning up

then i work on the the structure, ask claude for refinements, rewrite some parts and publish... that's a full article, under an hour

when you speak, you don't overthink

that directness hits different because readers can feel it... there's a natural rhythm in spoken thought that you cannot recreate by typing carefully, no matter how good you are

been running this system on desktop and iphone for months, Wispr Flow just launched on android too, so it works on every device now

if you create content and you still spend more time staring at a blank page than actually producing...

speak your next article, your best writing was never in your fingers, it was always in your voice
